item.title: Photosynthetic chimeric stem cells function as mitochondrial batteries
item.description: Therapies built on mitochondrial transfer hold promise for repairing dysfunctional, energy-deficient cells. Still, mesenchymal stem cells used as mitochondrial donors are limited by poor engraftment, risk of aberrant differentiation, and low transfer efficiency. Herein, we constructed photosynthesis-empowered cross-kingdom chimeric stem cells (PCSs; “mitochondrial battery”) by introducing plant-derived thylakoid-based artificial nuclei plus FGF21 -encoding messenger RNA (mRNA) into enucleated bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. Photosynthetic activity enhances mitochondrial transfer to restore metabolism in damaged cells and elevates anabolism to increase FGF21 production. Sustained FGF21 release promotes mitochondrial biogenesis and sustains long-term cellular energy homeostasis. Mouse and porcine wound healing models demonstrate that PCSs recharge cellular energy to accelerate wound repair. This light-activated cellular photosynthetic platform supports modular mRNA programmability, shows no engraftment or aberrant differentiation, and allows repeated administration for diverse therapeutic applications.

item.title: Alleviating the stability-energy density dilemma via electron-donor-mediated orbital symmetry regulation in sodium phosphate cathodes
item.description: Manganese-based sodium super ionic conductor-type cathode materials, leveraging the multielectron redox activity of manganese, represent a promising pathway toward high-energy-density sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). However, the unavoidable generation of Mn 3+ (3d 4 ) species during charge-discharge processes, characterized by asymmetric e g orbital occupancy, triggers octahedral symmetry breaking. This inherent electronic structural instability creates a fundamental contradiction between achieving high energy density and ensuring long cycle life that remains inherently difficult to reconcile. Here, we report an electron-donor–mediated (EDM) mechanism that suppresses Mn 3+ -induced octahedral distortion while preserving high-spin functionality. As electron-donating Fe 3+ and V 3+ are incorporated, Mn 3+ 3d electrons undergo partial delocalization. This electronic redistribution promotes orbital interactions between neighboring transition metal sites through the transition metal-oxygen framework, driving the e g orbitals toward a more symmetric occupation and suppressing octahedral distortion. The EDM-modified cathode demonstrates a high energy density of 492.06 Wh kg −1 . It delivers 178.8 mAh g −1 at 0.1 C and retains 80.2% of its capacity over 2000 cycles at 10 C, paving a novel pathway toward next-generation high-performance SIBs cathode materials.

item.title: Engineering a closed-loop electrochemical pathway for cadmium recovery and aqueous battery reutilization
item.description: Cadmium (Cd) waste is an unavoidable toxic by-product of zinc processing, but its electrochemical reutilization remains limited by the lack of routes that couple selective recovery with stable metal-anode operation. Here, we report a closed-loop electrochemical strategy that transforms model Cd-containing waste electrolytes into regenerable aqueous Cd metal anodes. A three-step potential-programmed electrodeposition process selectively recovers Cd while constructing compact Cd(002)-textured electrodes with tunable areal capacity. To preserve this recovered structure during cycling, cesium iodide is introduced to reconstruct the Cd-electrolyte interface, enabling iodide-dominated and cesium-assisted regulation of desolvation, ion flux, corrosion, and Cd growth. The resulting Cd anode achieves 99.98% average Coulombic efficiency and stable high-rate plating/stripping. Cd||I 2 coin and pouch cells validate full-cell operation under high loading and reduced excess Cd. Failed Cd anodes can be reextracted, regenerated, and reused, completing a recovery-operation-regeneration loop.

item.title: A unified lattice–surface engineering strategy stabilizing oxygen redox in Li-rich cathodes for all-solid-state batteries
item.description: Li-rich Mn-based layered oxides (LRMOs) are promising high-energy cathodes for all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), but their application is limited by irreversible O 2 evolution during lattice O 2− /O 2 2− redox and interfacial degradation at high voltages. Here we report a “coat–sinter–wash” synthetic strategy that simultaneously modulates bulk oxygen redox and stabilizes the cathode surface. An ammonium tungstate precursor is first coated onto LRMO particles. The subsequent sintering generates Li vacancies and enables W incorporation into the lattice, which acts as a “chemical rivet” and enhances the reversibility of lattice oxygen redox. A final washing step reconstructs the Li-deficient surface into an in-situ spinel layer, suppressing oxygen release from the surface and mitigating structural decomposition. The resulting ASSBs achieve remarkable cycling stability with 80% capacity retention over 500 cycles (0.5 C, 25°C) and an outstanding reversible capacity of 278.2 mAh g −1 (0.1 C, 40°C). Furthermore, an all-solid-state pouch cell with Si anode demonstrates an areal capacity of 4.55 mAh cm −2 and a high energy density of 543 Wh kg −1 . This work provides a scalable synthetic framework for stabilizing oxygen-redox cathodes in solid-state batteries.

item.title: Multiplexed and implantable fiber sensor for real-time blood monitoring
item.description: Accurate and real-time monitoring of blood electrolyte composition, particularly sodium (Na + ) and potassium (K + ), is crucial for guiding intraoperative and postoperative decisions, as these ions regulate critical bodily functions such as cardiac rhythm and fluid balance. Current blood analysis relies on ex vivo blood sampling, which introduces substantial time delays and can be susceptible to inaccuracies caused by temperature fluctuations. To address these challenges, we report here a multiplexed and implantable fiber sensor (MIFS) capable of monitoring Na + and K + ions in real time directly in the bloodstream. MIFS integrates three parallel liquid metal channels with a multilayer surface-electrode architecture, which synergistically enhances sensitivity, minimizes sensing drift, ensures mechanical flexibility, and offers outstanding biocompatibility for vascular implantation. In vivo testing in rabbit models and validation in human blood samples demonstrate MIFS’s superior sensing accuracy, real-time, and stable sensing in agreement with conventional ex vivo measurements. This work paves the way for real-time blood monitoring in clinical practice.

item.title: Magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber for deformation-resilient and smart electronic textiles
item.description: Electronic textiles represent a transformative platform for integrating technology into daily wear, yet their development has been undermined by a fundamental challenge: the conflicting requirements between mechanical deformation for functionality and structural stability for performance. This challenge is particularly acute in cylindrical fiber electrodes, where inherent nonuniform electric field distribution leads to dendrite formation and poor active material utilization-problems that are further exacerbated by mechanical deformation. Here, we present a magneto-mechano-electrochemical architecture that addresses this challenge. Through magnetoelectrochemistry, magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber promotes uniform electrochemical reactions, extending the battery lifespan by (374 ± 79)% and enhancing the capacity by (61 ± 20)% at a current density of 1.0 ampere per gram in the undeformed state. The magnetic field remains effective in regulating ion transport and stabilizing electrode structure under deformation. This deformation-resilient platform simultaneously enables energy harvesting from body motion and physiological monitoring through electromagnetic induction and magnetoelastic sensing, thereby transforming conventional textiles into deformation-resilient and smart health monitoring systems.

item.title: Nanoconfinement-cooperated catalysis enables rapid tandem redox kinetics for wide-temperature lithium-sulfur batteries
item.description: The slow kinetics of sulfur cathodes caused by the high energy barriers of Li + desolvation stem primarily from the structure of the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP). Herein, a synergistic strategy combining electrochemical tandem catalysis with spatial nanoconfinement is proposed to regulate the Li(solvent) x + dynamics. As a proof-of-concept, the porous covalent organic framework (denoted as TPBD) decorated MXene is in situ constructed, acting as a tandem kinetic promoter. The theoretical simulations and in situ Raman reveal that the porous TPBD layer confines the bulky Li(solvent) x + species and sieves the spatial structure with accelerated Li + diffusion kinetics. Meanwhile, MXene serves as a negatively charged substrate that helps disrupt anion-solvent interactions and reconstruct the solvation structure at the IHP, thereby enhancing Li + kinetics and sulfur redox reversibility. Encouragingly, the assembled cells demonstrate a superior Li + transference number (0.77), long-term cycling lifespan up to 1000 cycles, as well as excellent areal capacity (>6 mAh cm −2 ) at 0°C and superior rate capability at 50°C under a high sulfur loading of 7.51 mg cm −2 . The as-prepared pouch cell remains stable for over 100 cycles, validating this novel integration of catalysis and nanoconfinement for tandem kinetics in Li-S batteries.

item.title: Costly missed connections: Visitation and misconduct in California prisons
item.description: Social isolation is a major public health crisis with particularly deleterious consequences for vulnerable populations including incarcerated people. Theoretically, visitation from family should reduce social isolation and improve outcomes among incarcerated people, but existing quasi-experimental research provides limited support for the relationship between visitation and in-custody outcomes. We revisit the effect of visitation on in-custody misconduct-an important but administratively defined measure of institutional safety-by exploiting the fact that fluctuations in gasoline prices create unanticipated shifts in visitation uncorrelated with other factors associated with misconduct. We combine this quasi-experimental variation with smartphone mobility data identifying prison visits from cell phone pings and administrative data on misconduct in California prisons. We find that increases in visits induced by changes in transportation costs are negatively related to misconduct (particularly use-of-force events and personal battery), with effects concentrated immediately after visitation. Although the policy implications are subtle, these findings suggest that some strategies that reduce visitation barriers could be cost-effective ways to reduce prison violence. More broadly, they suggest that social connections have causal repercussions for violence and safety in extreme institutional environments.
